title: HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)
summary: Specifies HKDF, a key derivation function built on HMAC. It can be used as a building block in many protocols and applications, taking some initial keying material and producing strong keys. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It turns one secret into many different keys, like turning one lump of dough into several differently shaped cookies.

questions: how to derive keys with hmac
how does hkdf extract and expand work
should i use hkdf for passwords
what is the salt in hkdf
subtitle: A simple recipe for turning one source of secret key material into as many strong keys as a protocol needs.

tldr.problem: Protocols often start with key material that is not uniformly random, such as a Diffie-Hellman value, and need several cryptographically strong keys from it. Each protocol was inventing its own way to do this.
tldr.mechanism: HKDF works in two stages. Extract uses HMAC to concentrate the input keying material into a fixed-length pseudorandom key, and Expand uses HMAC again to stretch that key into as many output octets as needed.
tldr.outcome: It documents one general-purpose key derivation function to discourage a proliferation of KDF mechanisms. It is not meant to change existing protocols, and it is not designed for low-entropy secrets such as passwords.

today: RFC 5869 is an Informational RFC and, per the registry metadata, it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It remains the document that defines HKDF.

sections.title: Why a Key Derivation Function
sections.content:
A key derivation function (KDF) takes some initial keying material and derives from it one or more cryptographically strong secret keys. RFC 5869 specifies a simple KDF built on HMAC, named HKDF, which is already used in several IETF protocols, including IKEv2, PANA and EAP-AKA.

The purpose is to document it in a general way so that future protocols can adopt it and to discourage the proliferation of multiple KDF mechanisms. The RFC says plainly that it is not a call to change existing protocols and does not change or update any specification that already uses this KDF.

HKDF follows the extract-then-expand paradigm. The RFC notes that some other KDF specifications only cover the second stage, or do not separate the two stages, which often leads to design shortcomings.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you have one secret and need many different keys from it. HKDF is a shared, tested recipe for doing that, so nobody has to invent their own.

sections.title: Extract and Expand
sections.content:
Extract takes an optional salt and the input keying material (IKM) and computes PRK = HMAC-Hash(salt, IKM). The result is a pseudorandom key of HashLen octets. Note that the IKM is the HMAC input here, not the HMAC key. If no salt is given, it is set to a string of HashLen zeros. The goal is to concentrate possibly dispersed entropy into a short, strong key, even when an attacker knows or partly controls some of the input.

Expand takes the PRK (at least HashLen octets), an optional info string and the desired length L in octets, which must be at most 255*HashLen. It computes blocks T(1) = HMAC-Hash(PRK, T(0) | info | 0x01), T(2) = HMAC-Hash(PRK, T(1) | info | 0x02) and so on, where T(0) is empty and the counter is a single octet. The output keying material (OKM) is the first L octets of the concatenated blocks.

When the input is already a good pseudorandom key, the extract stage is not necessary and Expand can be used alone.
sections.eli5: First you mix your messy secret into one smooth, strong key. Then you use that key, plus a label saying what the new key is for, to make as many new keys as you like.

sections.title: Using Salt and Info Well
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC is a set of guiding principles. Salt is optional so that HKDF works where none is available, but the RFC stresses that using one adds significantly to strength. A salt is non-secret and can be reused. Ideally it is a random or pseudorandom string of length HashLen, but even a shorter or lower-quality salt helps. It must not be chosen or manipulated by an attacker; in IKE, for example, the salt comes from nonces that are authenticated first.

The info input is optional but often of great importance. It binds the derived keys to application and context, such as a protocol number, algorithm identifiers or user identities, so the same IKM used in different contexts does not yield the same keys. The one technical requirement is that info be independent of the IKM.

If the input is a Diffie-Hellman value, the extract step SHOULD NOT be skipped, because that value is not a uniformly random string. Using PRK directly as the output when L is no more than HashLen is NOT RECOMMENDED, since it would omit info.
sections.eli5: The salt is like a pinch of random spice that makes your recipe come out differently from everyone else's. The info label says which dish the key is for, so two dishes never get the same key.

sections.title: Limits and Security Considerations
sections.content:
HKDF is meant for many uses: building pseudorandom generators from imperfect randomness sources, deriving keys from a shared Diffie-Hellman value, deriving symmetric keys in hybrid public-key encryption, and key derivation for key wrapping.

It is not meant for deriving keys from a low-entropy source such as a password. The extract step can concentrate existing entropy but cannot amplify it, and password-based KDFs need an intentional slowdown to hinder dictionary attacks, which HKDF does not include. The RFC points such applications to PKCS #5 (RFC 2898).

The security discussion is short and defers to the published HKDF paper. It states that the analysis does not imply absolute security of any scheme and depends heavily on the strength of the underlying hash function and on modeling choices.
sections.eli5: HKDF is great at stretching a good secret, but it cannot make a weak secret strong. A short, easy password stays easy to guess no matter how you mix it.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content: Appendix A gives seven test cases so implementers can check their code. They cover SHA-256 and SHA-1, short and long inputs and outputs, zero-length salt and info, and one case where the salt is not provided and defaults to HashLen zero octets. For example, the first SHA-256 case has a 22-octet IKM, a 13-octet salt, a 10-octet info and L = 42, and yields a 32-octet PRK and a 42-octet OKM.
sections.eli5: These are practice problems with the answers included, so you can check that your own version gives the right result.
